Title: Causal Processes, Fitness, and the Differential Persistence of Lineages
URL: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/philosophy-of-science/article/abs/causal-processes-fitness-and-the-differential-persistence-of-lineages/ED4C33B07AF9567271B97BC87DF4F83A
Published: N/A
Author: Frédéric Bouchard
Highlights:
Ecological fitness has been suggested to provide a unifying definition of fitness. However, a metric for this notion of fitness was in most cases unavailable except by proxy with differential reproductive success. In this article, I show how differential persistence of lineages can be used as a way to assess ecological fitness. This view is inspired by a better understanding of the evolution of some clonal plants, colonial organisms, and ecosystems. Differential persistence shows the limitation of an ensemblist noncausal understanding of evolution. Causal explanations are necessary to understand the evolution by natural selection of these biological systems.

Title: Community coalescence: an eco-evolutionary perspective
URL: https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rstb.2019.0252
Published: N/A
Author: Castledine Meaghan ,  
    Sierocinski Pawel ,  
    Padfield Daniel  and  
    Buckling Angus
Highlights:
Community coalescence, the mixing of different communities, is widespread throughout microbial ecology. Coalescence can result in approximately equal contributions from the founding communities or dominance of one community over another. These different outcomes have ramifications for community structure and function in natural communities, and the use of microbial communities in biotechnology and medicine. However, we have little understanding of when a particular outcome might be expected. Here, we integrate existing theory and data to speculate on how a crucial characteristic of microbial communities—the type of species interaction that dominates the community—might affect the outcome of microbial community coalescence. Given the often comparable timescales of microbial ecology and microevolution, we explicitly consider ecological and evolutionary dynamics, and their interplay, in determining coalescence outcomes.
...
Community assembly, the process by which species colonise and interact with each other to establish a community, is shaped through ecological and evolutionary selection, drift and immigration [[1](#RSTB20190252C1)]. In microbes, however, whole communities often migrate as a unit. The process of more than one community mixing has been termed ‘community coalescence’ [[2](#RSTB20190252C2)]. Natural microbial communities frequently coalesce owing to abiotic (e.g. wind, tides or river flow) and biotic (e.g. animal courtship, parent–offspring interactions or leaves falling) factors [[2](#RSTB20190252C2)–[6](#RSTB20190252C6)]. Moreover, coalescence occurs owing to human activities such as industrial anaerobic digestion [[7](#RSTB20190252C7)], agriculture [[8](#RSTB20190252C8),[9](#RSTB20190252C9)] and between-human contact [[10](#RSTB20190252C10),[11](#RSTB20190252C11)] (e.g. romantic couples share similar oral microbiota through kissing [[12](#RSTB20190252C12)]).
...
The outcomes of coalescence can be grouped across two main categories ([figure1](#RSTB20190252F1)), which describe the composition and distribution of interactions of the coalesced community. Based on the prevalence of the members of the communities which coalesce, there can be a continuum between symmetric and asymmetric outcomes (equal contribution or dominance of one community). In asymmetrical outcomes, one community can be classed as ‘dominant’ if the sum of its populations are much greater than the other community and/or if it has more species [[7](#RSTB20190252C7),[13](#RSTB20190252C13)–[18](#RSTB20190252C18)] ([figure1](#RSTB20190252F1)). In symmetrical outcomes, the initial communities contribute approximately equally to the resultant coalesced community. The outcome of community coalescence can also be described in terms of the interactions between species of the mixed communities: a continuum ranging from chimeric to modular ([figure1](#RSTB20190252F1)). In chimeric coalescence, there is a high number of new interactions between members of different input communities. By contrast, in modular coalescence, interactions within input communities are preserved with fewer new interactions.
...
In nature, most coalescence events occur with one community immigrating into a new environment where there is a resident community present. Here, we would expect asymmetrical coalescence outcomes in favour of the resident versus immigrating community. This resident advantage can arise as a consequence of ecological and evolutionary processes. First, the resident community is likely to be much more abundant and have monopolized available resources, limiting an invader's success (priority effects) [[25](#RSTB20190252C25)]. Second, resident species are likely to be locally adapted to the niches present, owing to ecological selection (i.e. species sorting) and evolution, and hence have ‘home advantage’ over invaders [[1](#RSTB20190252C1),[11](#RSTB20190252C11),[26](#RSTB20190252C26)–[28](#RSTB20190252C28)].
...
However, this simple prediction does not take into account structural differences between communities' species interaction networks. Diversifying selection can reduce competition between co-occurring species by favouring resource specialization [[44](#RSTB20190252C44),[45](#RSTB20190252C45)]. Consequently, competition (on average) may be lower between species from the same versus different communities. In this way, the success of one species can indirectly benefit members of the same community during coalescence (co-selection) [[7](#RSTB20190252C7),[17](#RSTB20190252C17),[43](#RSTB20190252C43),[46](#RSTB20190252C46)]. By minimizing competition through resource specialization, communities become more ‘niche-packed’ and are expected to monopolize total resources more efficiently; the dominant community following coalescence should be the most productive of the input communities [[13](#RSTB20190252C13)]. Moreover, weaker competitive interactions may promote the community's structural stability: the breadth of ecological interactions under which species can coexist [[47](#RSTB20190252C47),[48](#RSTB20190252C48)]. This stability arises from greater within- versus between-species competition, meaning that if species reach a low frequency, they will experience relatively little competition and consequently increase in frequency (negative frequency dependent selection [[49](#RSTB20190252C49)]). Taken together, for communities dominated by competitive interactions, longer coevolution within a community is expected to promote dominance during coalescence.
...
53](#RSTB20190252C53),[90](#RSTB20190252C90)]. Mutualistic coevolution has been shown between two species, including a methanogen, where one species’ waste products (which inhibit its growth) are metabolized by the other species ([figure3](#RSTB20190252F3)*a*) [[53](#RSTB20190252C53)]. In coalescence of complex biomethane communities, consistent taxonomic dominance of the most productive community suggests that mutualists are co-selected and cohesively compete for resources ([figure3](#RSTB20190252F3)*b*,*c*) [[7](#RSTB20190252C7)]. As mentioned previously, competitive interactions also exist in these complex communities and thus the relative importance of mutualisms and competition in this coalescence example is unclear. Additionally, diseased gut microbiomes have been successfully cured using faecal transplants but not with probiotics [[16](#RSTB20190252C16),[19](#RSTB20190252C19)]. Functioning gut microbiomes rely on diverse species and network interactions, especially mutualisms, which are provided by faecal transplants as network interactions can be retained to facilitate an asymmetric treatment outcome [[16](#RSTB20190252C16),[19](#RSTB20190252C19),[91](#RSTB20190252C91)]. Further support comes from an*in vitro*study which
...
However, both theoretical and empirical research is greatly lacking, meaning many of these predictions are highly speculative. To date, theory of competition in coalescence is the most developed [[13](#RSTB20190252C13),[43](#RSTB20190252C43),[54](#RSTB20190252C54)–[57](#RSTB20190252C57)] but more attention is warranted to trophic and mutualistic interactions ([table1](#RSTB20190252TB1)) [[7](#RSTB20190252C7),[15](#RSTB20190252C15)]. Experiments with synthetic systems can be used to understand the mechanisms underlying coalescence [[92](#RSTB20190252C92),[93](#RSTB20190252C93)], while natural communities address whether results are ecologically relevant [[7](#RSTB20190252C7),[8](#RSTB20190252C8),[55](#RSTB20190252C55),[56](#RSTB20190252C56),[94](#RSTB20190252C94)]. Some microbial systems have been studied in the context of hosts, such as locusts [[95](#RSTB20190252C95)] or plant species [[28](#RSTB20190252C28),[96](#RSTB20190252C96)], to examine between-microbiome dynamics and implications on host health. Owing to the complexity of microbial communities, we would encourage future research to explore a breadth of interaction types which could influence coalescence outcomes.

The extent to which natural ecosystems might evolve by natural selection depends on the extent to which vertical inheritance exists and dominates over natural processes, such as priority effects on ecosystem assembly, sampling variation during assembly, horizonal migration between ecosystems, and variability in the capacity of descendent system to inherit critical biotic and abiotic material pro duced by niche construction activities. Ecosystems in nature may behave more like horizontally acquired micro biomes, in which one lineage (often and sometimes arbi trarily designated the host or a foundation species) recruits other lineages by a combination of direct (organ ism-organism recognition processes) and indirect meth ods analogous to “ecosystem engineering.” Given that community heritability does not indicate the level at which fitness variation might be relevant to ENS, we advocate for caution in extrapolating H 2 C from common garden experiments to natural systems. In the simple case of individual selection within a single (enduring) commu nity, species will interact and influence each other’s fitness landscape (Fig. 1C). Genetic variation within such species can be the target of individual selection, and in that case, those species would coevolve. While the IIGEs within such a community can change over time according to this pro cess, there is no re-productive (Fig. 1A) or reproductive (Fig. 1B) feedback affecting a distribution of IIGEs across a larger set of communities, so those IIGEs cannot be the target of selection at the community level. Nevertheless, positive H 2 C could be obtained from common garden experiments for any species-level polymorphisms that happen to be associated with some aspect of within community composition. Here, broad sense heritability would be a poor predictor of any response to within community ENS. A narrower sense of heritability would be more suited to this setting. For selection to produce an evolutionary sorting of alternative systems of IIGEs, there must be some mecha nism whereby fitness effects (individual level in MLS1 or community level in MLS2) can feed back to a distribution of IIGEs among groups (Fig. 1 A or B). In case of MLS2, vari ation in community traits captured by H 2 C can be directly transmitted to descendent communities if the foundation species is part of the transmission “propagule.” Here, since H 2 C does summarize genetically based interactions with potential to affect differential fitness at the group level, it should be a good predictor of the evolutionary response under MLS2, if this is imposed. Alternatively, in the case of MLS1, H 2 C can be interpreted as summarizing genetically based interactions with potential to feed back to individual-level fitness. However, since there is no commu nity inheritance mechanism for IIGEs in MLS1, the evolu tionary process depends on horizontal rather than vertical inheritance and fails to meet Lewontin’s heredity criterion. Nonetheless, through effects on individual-level fitness, an evolutionary response in the genetically based interactions between species is possible via MLS1. One implication is that sets of genes residing in different species could expe rience a degree of coordinated evolution [reminiscent of Dawkins’s “genes-as-oarsman” analogy (46)] according to the extent that their lower-level fitness effects are additive and are compatible with a given IIGE environment. The membership and stability of gene sets having such com munity genome dynamics should be the focus of future community genetics investigation. Foundation species play a role in community and eco system research very similar to that played by the host in “the hologenome theory of evolution” (73). Unsurprisingly, the objections to that claim (38, 74–76) focus on the prob lematic relationship between the re-production (rather than reproduction) of multispecies collectives and Lewon tin’s criteria. A solution might be realized in both settings if the standard view of ENS built around Lewontin’s recipe were replaced by David Hull’s replicator-interactor frame work (35, 55). In Hull’s conception of ENS, holistic interac tions between complex entities and their environment are the causal basis of differential fitness, which is manifested as differential reproduction of lower-level replicators. In such a framework, ephemeral entities like the ellipse in Fig. 1A illustrating MLS1 would be cast as “interactors” and could be organisms [as in Dawkins’s The Selfish Gene (46)] but could as well be communities or ecosystems, while the cog nate replicators could be genes (as in Dawkins’s book) but also organisms or species whose differential reproduction is facilitated by being part of a better-growing or more persis tent community or collective. Such a solution has been hinted at before and recently made more explicit (55, 77). Here, we develop this idea further by applying the replicator-interactor framework to IIGEs as an expansion of the extended pheno type concept to include multispecies MLS1. We acknowledge that multispecies interactions do occur within a single collec tive, and extended phenotypes can evolve by nothing more inclusive than individual selection and coevolution in this con text (Fig. 1C). Under MLS1, communities evolve as interactors, having unique IIGEs as potential targets of trait-group selec tion. The effects of IIGEs on individual fitness feed back to their distribution among communities. According to Hull’s replicator-interactor framework, this would lead to selection of beneficial IIGEs, and differential growth of communities (interactors) would cause differential survival and reproduc tion of those organisms (replicators) most relevant to benefi cial community-level interactions. The advantage of switching to the replicator-interactor framework is that it can accommo date IIGEs that coordinate community composition without requiring all populations to have unified fitness gain. The foundation population can cultivate a community where only some of the populations have a fitness gain or even none other than itself. The hierarchical structure of MLS models allows for a variety of evolutionary processes to operate concurrently across levels (55). Indeed, organismal coevolution is expected to occur in MLS1 whenever organism generation times permit mutation-drift-selection dynamics to play out within the lifespan of a community. Title: Evolution and Community Assembly Across Spatial Scales | Annual Reviews
URL: https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-ecolsys-102220-024934
Published: 2022-11-02T00:00:00.000Z
Author: Mathew A. Leibold|Lynn Govaert|Nicolas Loeuille|Luc De Meester|Mark C. Urban
Highlights:
The finding that adaptive evolution can often be substantial enough to alter ecological dynamics challenges traditional views of community ecology that ignore evolution. Here, we propose that evolution might commonly alter both local and regional processes of community assembly. We show how adaptation can substantially affect community assembly and that these effects depend on regional (metacommunity) factors, including environmental heterogeneity and its spatial structure. In particular, early colonists can often arrive from a nearby community, adapt to local conditions, and subsequently alter the establishment or abundance of late-arriving species, often producing an evolutionary priority effect. We also discuss how interaction type and relative rates of colonization, evolution, and community interactions determine divergent community outcomes. We describe new conceptual approaches that provide insights into these dynamics and statistical methods that can better evaluate their importance. Overall, we demonstrate that accounting for adaptation during community assembly opens up novel ways for making progress on fundamental questions in community ecology.

Title: Species colonisation, not competitive exclusion, drives community overdispersion over long-term succession
URL: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ele.12476
Published: N/A
Author: Allan, E.
Highlights:
Ecological communities often transition from phylogenetic and functional clustering to overdispersion over succession as judged by space-for-time substitution studies. Such a pattern has been generally attributed to the increase in competitive exclusion of closely related species with similar traits through time, although colonisation and extinction have rarely been examined. Using 44 years of uninterrupted old-field succession in New Jersey, USA, we confirmed that phylogenetic and functional clustering decreased as succession unfolded, but the transition was largely driven by colonisation. Early colonists were closely related and functionally similar to residents, while later colonists became less similar to the species present. Extirpated species were generally more distantly related to residents than by chance, or exhibited random phylogenetic/functional patterns, and their relatedness to residents was not associated with time. These results provide direct evidence that the colonisation of distant relatives, rather than extinction of close relatives, drives phylogenetic and functional overdispersion over succession.

Title: Spatiotemporal dimensions of community assembly
URL: https://esj-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1438-390X.12144
Published: N/A
Author: Abbott, B. W.
Highlights:
Community assembly is a series of species filtering processes from a regional species pool to local communities (Belyea && Lancaster,[1999](#pope12144-bib-0008); HilleRisLambers et al.,[2012](#pope12144-bib-0053); Keddy,[1992](#pope12144-bib-0058)), illuminating the complex nature of how species interact with the environment. Local communities are firstly shaped by “dispersal,” through which the members of a regional species pool are sorted by colonization processes. Colonized species are further selected by “abiotic” and “biotic” filters, which select species that are able to maintain sustainable population sizes in a local community. Species composition in each locality also exhibits spatiotemporal variations due to “ecological drift,” which refers to stochasticity caused by demographic processes. As such, community assembly is a sequential processes of dispersal, abiotic and biotic filtering, and ecological drift.
...
After decadal debates on which viewpoint can adequately dictate biodiversity patterns in nature (Condit et al.,[2002](#pope12144-bib-0026); McGill,[2003](#pope12144-bib-0070)), there is a general agreement that neither of these viewpoints solely explain community assembly (Gilbert && Lechowicz,[2004](#pope12144-bib-0045); Tuomisto et al.,[2003](#pope12144-bib-0113)). Rather, multiple processes act in concert to assemble ecological communities (Adler et al.,[2007](#pope12144-bib-0002); Gravel et al.,[2006](#pope12144-bib-0048)); this finding has motivated researchers to explore their relative importance in natural ecosystems (Chase && Myers,[2011](#pope12144-bib-0022); Peres-Neto et al.,[2006](#pope12144-bib-0087); Box[1](#pope12144-fea-0001)). However, a primary mechanism that controls assembly processes greatly varies across study systems and taxa (Cottenie,[2005](#pope12144-bib-0029); Iwamoto et al.,[2022](#pope12144-bib-0122); Soininen et al.,[2007](#pope12144-bib-0102)), and this contingent nature of ecological systems has challenged community ecologists (Belyea && Lancaster,[1999](#pope12144-bib-0008); Lawton,[1999](#pope12144-bib-0062); Simberloff,[2004](#pope12144-bib-0100)). The apparent dearth of general rules is partly due to the considerable variation of ecological contexts across studies. As such, a key quest for modern community ecology is to “map” the community assembly rules onto dimensions that are common across study systems and taxa (Chase,[2003](#pope12144-bib-0018)). This approach will help transform community ecology into a more predictive science with the potential to address the contingent nature of community ecology. As a sufficient number of case studies have been cataloged over the past decades, classifying individual findings into common and idiosyncratic patterns has the potential to draw generalizations (Simberloff,[2004](#pope12144-bib-0100)).
...
Among statistical tools, null modeling and variation partitioning are the two common approaches found in community ecology to disentangle the relative contributions of multiple assembly processes. Null model analyses assess whether the observed patterns deviate from chance expectations (Nakadai et al.,[2018](#pope12144-bib-0080); Nakadai && Kawakita,[2017](#pope12144-bib-0081)). In the context of community assembly, such a deviation is interpreted as a sign of “nonrandom” ecological processes. For example, if a pair of species co-occur less often than expected by a given null model, they may interact negatively (e.g., competition) or may prefer distinct habitats. Conversely, more frequent co-occurrence than random expectation implies positive interactions or similar habitat preferences of the two species. Connor and Simberloff ([1979](#pope12144-bib-0027)) represents a notable instance of null model analysis in community assembly studies. They argued that the “checkerboard” distribution of avian species found in the Bismarck Archipelago (i.e., species*A*is absent from an island where species*B*is present, and vice versa) is expected by chance alone, as opposed to the former claim of Diamond ([1975](#pope12144-bib-0142)) that ecological mechanisms are responsible for this pattern to emerge. Similar analysis can be performed at the community-level by examining whether the observed site-to-site dissimilarity of species composition (i.e., β-diversity) is larger (i.e., overdispersion) or smaller (i.e., clustering) than random expectations (Chase && Myers,[2011](#pope12144-bib-0022)). It is important to note, however, that null model analysis cannot identify specific mechanisms that cause the deviation from random expectations. Overdispersion may be a collective outcome of ecological interactions among species and differences in species' preferences for abiotic environments. Similarly, clustering patterns can emerge through multiple mechanisms, including mutualistic interspecific interactions, shared environmental preferences, or limited dispersal (Chase && Myers,[2011](#pope12144-bib-0022)).

For instance, a spatially constrained permutation test can deal with its sensitivity to spatial autocorrelation of environments that falsely inflates the explanatory capacity of environmental components (Clappe et al.,[2018](#pope12144-bib-0024)). More specifically, the effects of environmental shifts on assembly processes are also dependent on the degree of congruence between past and present community structures. If long-lived individuals can persist in a site though the environment changes, it would result in a mismatch between community composition and contemporary environment, leading to (apparently) weaker abiotic filtering. Several studies showed that the explanatory power of environmental variables for species composition was larger for juvenile trees than for adults (Punchi-Manage et al.,[2014](#pope12144-bib-0090); Thonhofer et al.,[2015](#pope12144-bib-0110)), consistent with the prediction that current environments are not good predictors of species composition of long-lived organisms. Although the persistence of individuals could be an essential factor in mediating the effect of abiotic filtering (Nakadai,[2020](#pope12144-bib-0077)), few studies have explicitly incorporated this idea into an analytical framework. An interesting avenue of future research is to explore how individual persistence influences the importance of different assembly processes, such as abiotic and biotic filtering, dispersal, and ecological drift (Costa-Pereira et al.,[2022](#pope12144-bib-0028); Nakadai,[2021](#pope12144-bib-0078),[2022](#pope12144-bib-0079)).

In this review, we synthesized how the influences of the assembly processes vary systematically along some of the spatiotemporal dimensions. Our review is an important first step to generalizing the concepts of community assembly across taxa and systems; indeed, we found some consistent patterns along the dimensions. Therefore, mapping assembly processes to spatiotemporal dimensions may help predict which ecological mechanisms are most influential (Figure[1](#pope12144-fig-0001)). The spatial and temporal scales and complexity could resolve the contingency of community assembly rules on study systems that have been widely observed (Cottenie,[2005](#pope12144-bib-0029); Graco-Roza et al.,[2022](#pope12144-bib-0129); Soininen et al.,[2007](#pope12144-bib-0102)) and challenged researchers (Belyea && Lancaster,[1999](#pope12144-bib-0008); Lawton,[1999](#pope12144-bib-0062); Simberloff,[2004](#pope12144-bib-0100)).

It is also a clade in that it consists of whichever aspen tree was first (the ancestor, whether or not still alive) and all its descendants, liv ing or dead. Pando as a collective persists in part because it is so vast and variable. It currently weighs about 13 million pounds and occupies more than 100 acres (as cited in Bouchard 2008). It becomes, Bouchard argues, increasingly fit (more robust and resilient) over time as a persister because of evolution by differential reproduction of some of its parts (some of those 45,000 trees). That is, such persisters display adaptive change as a response to the selective pressures from their envi ronments and these changes [at the particle level] accumulate and are fine-tuned over time, which results in an increase in the system’s [the collective persister’s] capacity to survive. This adaptive change occurs in response to selection on the parts of the system. However these systems’ evolution is not adequately captured by a concept of evolutionary fitness that is defined solely in terms of differential reproductive success. (Bouchard 2008, 562) Putting flesh on these bones is one of my goals in this chapter. Indeed, as a clone or clade, Pando as a whole does not reproduce, by definition. Its parts do, though. A model might be a clone in a chemostat (Neto and Doo little 2022). In an ideal chemostat, all cells are descendant from a single cell at some time in the past. A clone is a clade, in other words, and it persists, accumulating mutations that allow for better and better chemostat growth, selected for among its cells in reproductive competition. One might define the population in which the current Pando is the winner as including all the earlier and less ecologically fit Pandos. One would get into trouble, nev ertheless, by attempting to deal with Pando as a whole as if the collective exhibited inheritance (Bouchard 2011). Without reproducing, Pando
...
Many mainstream neo-Darwinists will admit, grudgingly, that differential persistence can be a mechanism for ENS. But, as noted, they will deny that it can lead very far or that it is very “interesting.” Samir Okasha (2003, 747) asserts: So while differential clade survival may well have been a transforming factor in biotic evolution, from the viewpoint of a theory of selection it is not an interest ing phenomenon. It cannot lead to clade adaptations, since adaptation requires cumulative selection, hence reproduction. Similarly, PGS (2009, 105) argues that “clades might be differentially eliminated, but that is not enough for a significant Darwinian process.” He observes that the real function of reproduction in the traditional ENS story is replenishment, which, if continued, can lead to complex adaptation or origin explanations. Without reproduction, there will be a smaller “plat form” for the next persistence-conferring “mutation” and an even smaller population for the next one after that. But such is not actually the case for clade selection, as detailed above and emphasized now. 9 Clades continuously spawn populations of species that compete to be ancestral to the whole clade in future. They do replen ish themselves, and this is what PGS asserts is the role of reproduction in his form of ENS. This competition may involve no direct interaction but still can be seen as limited by the carrying capacity of the environment, a plausibly zero-sum game (Hornborg 2009). One could say something like this for all Life as a whole but also—and over a much shorter timescale—for each clade within it. Mammalia remains quite robust as a clade, but few of the species that comprised Mammalia 100 million years ago are with us as subclades today, even with changed names. By the classical view, replication/reproduction of species (even if loosely defined, as above) can only produce “fortuitous by-products” at any higher level at which there is not reproduction. One solution is to add differen tial persistence to the means or products of classical ENS and multilevel selection theory. Another would be to adopt Hull’s two-thing formulation, because selection is redefined in a more persistence-friendly way in that formulation. Certainly, the persistence of Pando has to do with its favoring the replication of certain tree types. As PGS wrote (in defense of his classical theory and as already quoted in section 3.6): The important point is that it does not matter what is imagined at the lower level, because all we need is that reproduction lead to parent–offspring similarity at the level at which evolution is to occur. It does not matter what particular mechanism underlies the pattern of similarity, as long as the pattern is present. (Godfrey-Smith 2009, 33–34; emphasis mine) But what happens at lower levels does matter for complex adaptation—if it is (1) at that lower level that reproduction replenishes the supply of entities available for further innovation, (2) selection, albeit for persistence, occurs at a higher level, and (3) one buys into the general notion of ontologi cal dependence anyway. This last point means that nothing happens at a higher level that does not depend on change at a lower level—even if evolu tion is driven by selection at a higher level at which there is no reproductive replen ishment. If the ecological diversity of a clade depends on some lower-level genic mutation favoring greater evolvability (which surely it does), and the clade founded by the species in which that mutation occurs differentially survives because it is more diverse (which it logically might do), then there would be more species harboring that mutation than there would other wise be. This is true even if no single species specifically benefits by being a member of that clade and even if the possession of that particular muta tion was deleterious to individuals (which it could be). This is one of the meanings of “downward causation”: an increase in the number (and thus in the chance of finding) of lower-level units in consequence of selection at a higher level. 10 Donald Campbell (1974, 180) holds that this happens when “processes at the lower levels of a hierarchy are restrained by and act in conformity to the laws of the higher level.” So, in more down-to-earth terms, how has clade selection been cumu lative? Surely, during Life’s earliest history, its diversity increased. It must have been always (once it got started) sufficient to prevent total extinction by “impact frustration,” the constant early bombardment of the Earth by meteorites. That diversity and its potential to grow underwrite the faith that even we humans cannot extinguish all life on Earth. This growth has been documented by many expounders of the history of Life—for instance,
...
Richard Dawkins in his 2009 book The Greatest Show on Earth. And, of course, it is inevitable (McShea and Brandon 2010). We must realize that “com plex adaptation,” which Okasha suggested differential persistence could not accomplish, has a different meaning at the individual and the clade level. At the former, it results in such structures as the vertebrate eye, but for the latter it might be seen as biodiversity and the interconnectedness of species in the collection of local ecosystems and global biogeochemical processes that is Gaia. I will have more to say about this idea, which I owe to postdoc Celso Neto, in chapter 11. If we could extend the classical view of ENS to include differential per sistence, we might incorporate such selection into it. But clades are also persistent interactors, interacting with their environments quite broadly. The replicators that contribute to their “doing better” are the species that make them up. The traits listed in section 9.7 may not seem like typical interactions, but surely this reflects the contingent history by which we define that term.

Title: A unified framework for measuring selection on cellular lineages and traits | eLife
URL: https://elifesciences.org/articles/72299
Published: 2022-12-06T00:00:00.000Z
Author: Shunpei Yamauchi
Highlights:
As documented by many single-cell studies, phenotypic states of individual cells in cellular populations are heterogeneous and often correlate with fitness variations among cellular lineages (Balázsi et al., 2011; Elowitz et al., 2002; Kelly and Rahn, 1932; Powell, 1956; Wakamoto et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2010; Cerulus et al., 2016; Susman et al., 2018). Fitness heterogeneity within a population causes a statistical bias on ancestral cells’ contributions to the number of descendants, which is broadly referred to as ‘selection’ (Leibler and Kussell, 2010). Such bias from growth heterogeneity makes the relations between cellular lineages and populations nontrivial. For example, an intriguing consequence of intra-population selection is a growth rate gain, a phenomenon that cell population’s growth rate becomes greater than the mean division rate of isolated single-cell lineages (Powell, 1956; Hashimoto et al., 2016; Rochman et al., 2018). Recent progress of single-cell measurements has enabled high-throughput acquisitions of cellular lineage trees and historical dynamics in each lineage (Stewart et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2010; Hashimoto et al., 2016). However, establishing the theory and method of cellular lineage statistics to quantify fitness differences among different phenotypic states and intrapopulation selection is still in progress (Nozoe et al., 2017; García-García et al., 2019; Levien et al., 2020; Genthon and Lacoste, 2020; Genthon and Lacoste, 2021).
...
Fitness: In evolutionary biology, fitness refers to the expected per capita contribution of individuals of a particular trait (usually a genotype) to the future population (Futuyma, 2010). For example, if a set of N0 individuals with trait X produce N1 descendants on average in the future population, the fitness of this trait would be N1/N0. Since proliferation usually proceeds multiplicatively, the logarithm of fitness, In (N1/N0), is also often referred to as ‘fitness’. Analogously, in our framework we define fitness for cell lineage traits as the expected contribution of lineages with a given trait value in the future population. For each cell lineage σ, the number of cell divisions occurring along the lineage, D(σ), is used to estimate the expected contribution of each lineage to the future population.
...
Fitness landscape: In evolutionary biology, fitness landscapes are visual representations of relationships between reproductive abilities (fitness) and genotypes (Futuyma, 2010), where the height along the landscape corresponds to fitness. Since “genotype space” is vast and usually difficult to construct or visualize, fitness landscapes are often referred to as a metaphorical or conceptual tool for understanding complex evolutionary processes. For practical applications, however, fitness landscapes are often mapped on a low dimensional allele frequency space or a phenotypic space. Analogously, in our framework fitness landscapes are mapped on cell lineage trait spaces. However, they are different in that there is no assumption of genotypic differences underlying different trait states. Furthermore, the landscapes are directly measurable using cellular lineage trees and trait dynamics in each lineage.
...
For a cell lineage trait X, we define its fitness landscape to be a function h(x) that reports the expected reproductive success of lineages having trait value X=x. Each lineage σ having trait value x contributes 2D(σ) lineages to the future population, and by summing over lineages sharing the same trait value, we estimate the expected reproductive success of the trait and measure its fitness landscape. If differences in X correlate with division count heterogeneity among cell lineages, h(x) varies across the trait space of X; if differences in X are uncorrelated with division count heterogeneity, h(x) is constant over the entire space of X (Figure 2).
...
Selection: The term selection refers to processes in which the frequencies of individuals with different traits change due to differences in their fitness (Futuyma, 2010). In evolutionary biology, selection is usually assessed based on changes in the distribution of traits between two points in times, which requires an accurate measure of fitness and a model to determine whether the observed changes were the result of trait fitness differences. In our cell lineage statistics framework, we measure selection by determining whether the observed distribution of lineage traits (i.e. the retrospective distribution) differs from the distribution expected in the absence of fitness differences (i.e. the chronological distribution). The key advantage that lineage-based analysis provides is the ability to construct explicitly the chronological distribution, which is the natural ‘null hypothesis’ against which selection can be tested in a model-independent manner.
...
Selection strength: S[X] (i.e., SJF[X], SKL(1)[X], or SKL(2)[X]) is a quantitative measure that reports how strongly differences in the states of cell lineage trait X are correlated with cell lineage fitness, taking the distributions of X into account. The selection strength in our framework is measured by differences in the fitness measures or by differences between chronological and retrospective distributions (Equations 2–4). One can prove that these different definitions are mathematically equivalent.
...
An advantage of this framework is its independence from any growth and division models. The mechanisms driving the growth and division of individual cells are diverse among organisms. For example, the properties of cellular growth and division, such as whether a cell’s size increases exponentially or linearly and whether cell size regulation follows sizer or adder models, could depend on cell types, organisms, and environmental conditions (Jun et al., 2018; Kohram et al., 2021). Therefore, any model assumptions restrict applicability and necessitate model validation before application. The model independence of the framework presented here comes from the definitions of two essential quantities: the chronological and retrospective probabilities. Quantifying these probabilities requires only the information of the numbers of cells at initial and end time points and of division counts on each cellular lineage. Consequently, this formalism can be applied even to non-stationary conditions without modifications. However, we also remark that this independence from the details other than cell lineage structures imposes a limitation on the framework because it cannot report any potential influences from factors such as heterogeneous environments around cells and non-quantified traits. Furthermore, the fitness landscape h⁢(x) and the relative selection strength Srel⁢[X] evaluate only the correlations between the trait and fitness, not causal relationships. However, causal traits should have large selection strength values, and this framework helps narrow down the candidates for essential traits. Most importantly, division statistics is the focal information that connects molecular details underlying cellular growth and division to population growth. Regulatory mechanisms can influence population growth only by modulating the division statistics in a cellular population.
